summary: Episode 40 begins with World Cup fever as an example of how large the social impact of a public figure can be, then asks how we can make the Prophet Muhammad ﷺ felt by today's generation. The ustaz then continues the Isra' Mi'raj: a people who harvest instantly (the reward of spending multiplied 700 times, Al-Baqarah 261), linked to usury and charity in Al-Baqarah 276, the gap between rich and poor, consumerism and the need for critical thinking and living in line with the fitrah. The Prophet ﷺ also saw the river Al-Kawthar, linked to Surah Al-Kawthar, the beauty of Paradise with colours that have no name, the hadith qudsi 'what no eye has seen', and Malik, the keeper of Hell, who does not smile. The ustaz closes with sport as a way out for some poor children, the film Jhund, and the reality that prayer should have a social impact, citing Fiqh as-Salah (Al-Qaradawi) and The Muslim Worldview (Hamka).
keyPoints: The sirah is not a frozen subject: it has social impact, and we need to ask how the Prophet ﷺ can be felt as a role model by young people today.
The Prophet ﷺ saw a people who sowed and harvested instantly. Allah promises spending in His way at least 700-fold (Al-Baqarah 261), and spending includes wealth, energy, time and an ear to listen.
Usury is destroyed and charity is made to grow (Al-Baqarah 276). The ustaz links it to the gap between rich and poor, consumerism and systems that shape people as workers.
Muslims are called to think critically and live in line with the fitrah, and prayer trains us to cut distractions so we can think clearly.

The Prophet ﷺ saw Al-Kawthar, Sidrat al-Muntaha and the beauty of Paradise that 'no eye has seen, no ear has heard and no heart has conceived', and Malik, the keeper of Hell, who never smiles (a weak narration).
Prayer is not only a spiritual matter: the Quran says it prevents shameful and wrongful acts, so our prayer should leave a social impact.

books.context: An outline of the Muslim worldview on science, art, knowledge, beauty and the material. The ustaz began reading it around 2011 and mentions the chapter on prayer that describes it as a lighthouse for a lost ship.

A book on the wisdom of the legislation, the philosophy of prayer and the fiqh of every kind of prayer. The ustaz says the philosophy of prayer has gone missing from our understanding, and it is among the last books he had published.
Tells of a prison officer who was harsh when colleagues were present but privately apologised to Buya. The ustaz uses it to illustrate the angels of Hell, who are firm because of their duty.
books.note: Title not mentioned in the lecture.

books.context: Cited for the point that 700-fold in Al-Baqarah 261 is a minimum.
A series on history not taught in schools, including the education and work systems that shape people as industrial workers. The ustaz suggests looking for it and says it is heavy but useful.
Read by the ustaz to his child before bed, about poor Muslim children who play football and the prize of a ball for the highest literacy score.
books.note: The title in the transcript is unclear.

books.context: A true story of a retired professor who set up a slum football league in India to save children from drugs and crime. The ustaz took the Arba Foundation team to watch it before starting the Adiwira project.
The ustaz mentions a documentary showing that the wealth of Indonesia's 50 richest people could support the lives of 50 million people, as an example of the rich-poor gap.
Cited to show that human imagination is limited to what has been experienced, while Paradise is 'beyond human experience'.
Source of the Al-Kawthar hadith and the hadith qudsi on what is prepared for the righteous servant.
A collection of hadith with a dedicated chapter on spending and charity.
A commentary on Sahih Bukhari that discusses the Isra' Mi'raj hadith, including the river Al-Kawthar and Sidrat al-Muntaha.

people.context: Mentioned as an example of a sports figure with enormous influence worldwide. The ustaz cites the effect of his action on a drinks company's share price in 2021 as an example of social impact.
The ustaz mentions an unnamed university study showing Islamophobia and hate crime fell around his presence in Liverpool, and the stadium now provides a prayer room.
The son of an imam in Senegal who now builds hospitals, schools and roads in his village. An example of an athlete's social effect.
Said the darkest day in Madinah was the day the Prophet ﷺ died.
Explained to the Prophet ﷺ about the people who harvest, the river Al-Kawthar and Malik.
Cited for the point that 700-fold in Al-Baqarah 261 is a minimum, and Allah multiplies as He wills.
The ustaz recommends watching his history series for its deep thinking on education and economic systems.
An example of compassion in sport: the whole stadium prayed for him and opponents hugged him when his wife suffered a miscarriage.
Never smiles, reflecting Allah's wrath and the severity of His punishment. In a weak narration supported by a Quranic verse.
Author of The Muslim Worldview and a book on his experience in prison. The ustaz began reading his work through novels before the more important works.
Mentioned together with Ronaldo as figures followed by millions. The ustaz urges us to look at their difficult childhoods.
Author of Fiqh as-Salah, which discusses the wisdom and philosophy of the legislation of prayer.

lessons.title: The sirah is not a frozen subject
lessons.body: The sirah must be linked to today's social realities, not just read in a book without seeing its effect.

lessons.title: Make the Prophet ﷺ a role model who is truly felt
lessons.body: Many can write an essay 'my idol is the Messenger of Allah', but the ustaz invites us to ask how young people can feel his personality and strength as they feel their idols'.

lessons.title: The community needs many talents in many fields
lessons.body: Parents should not only want their children to be doctors or engineers. The community needs professional athletes and other fields because their social effect is large. The Prophet's ﷺ Companions also had varied expertise.

lessons.title: The Prophet ﷺ played every role, so losing him was the most devastating
lessons.body: An athlete plays one role, but the Prophet ﷺ was general, imam, educator, father and mentor. That is why losing him was the most devastating for the Companions.

lessons.title: Spending is not only money: energy, time and an ear
lessons.body: Offering an ear to listen to someone's problems is also spending that is multiplied if intended for Allah, because the minimum of 700 times is the lower limit, not the upper.

lessons.title: Spending and waqf are an economic framework, not just individual attitude
lessons.body: Education and medicine in Islamic civilisation were founded on waqf. The ustaz contrasts it with neoliberalism, which turns everything into business.

lessons.title: Usury destroys, charity makes grow
lessons.body: Allah uses the same root (yurbi) to show that what actually grows is charity, not usury. The ustaz cites studies showing high rich-poor gaps go together with crime.

lessons.title: Beware of consumerism that turns us into 'zombies'
lessons.body: Minimalism fails because technology increasingly pushes us to buy nonstop out of fear of missing out.

lessons.title: Question the systems we accept without thinking
lessons.body: Who set the eight-hour workday, all-day school, the syllabus and what goes in museums? A thinking community is one whose first revelation was 'read', not only reading texts but society and nature.

lessons.title: Live by the fitrah, including in neighbourhood design
lessons.body: Islamic cities used to arrange people of all ages in one area so the elderly were not left alone. The ustaz asks who decided that houses get smaller and hours get longer.

lessons.title: Prayer cuts distractions so we think clearly
lessons.body: In prayer we recite Allah's verses and give full attention. From there we begin to see wrongdoing that we had long treated as normal.

lessons.title: The sirah is a story of reform, not nostalgia
lessons.body: Not only for longing and weeping, but for how the Prophet ﷺ moved holistic and strategic change. The ustaz also criticises confining religion to the spiritual space alone.

lessons.title: Compassion, not hostility, when people suffer loss
lessons.body: Even in ancient wars generals sent condolences, and in sport opponents hug a player who has lost a child. The Quraysh, by contrast, cheered when the Prophet ﷺ lost a son.

lessons.title: Value varied talents and create a good environment
lessons.body: Judging only by exams wastes many talents. The ustaz reminds us we are responsible for creating an environment so young people do not fall into drugs, vaping and pornography.

lessons.title: Prayer should leave a social impact
lessons.body: The Quran says prayer prevents shameful and wrongful acts. The ustaz admits the prayer of many, himself included in the past, left no mark because it was narrowed to a private matter. It is also revealed in how children see prayer at home.

glossary.meaning: Deferring reward: the concept of worldly life, we sow, wait patiently and await the harvest, unlike the people who harvest instantly in the Mi'raj narration.
Success, from a word meaning farmer. We sow and are patient, and may not live to harvest the result.
Spending wealth, energy or time in Allah's way. The ustaz says it shares a root with 'nafaq' (tunnel), something hidden, which is also the root of munafiq.
Economic thinking that makes education and medicine for-profit businesses. The ustaz contrasts it with the past when they were seen as basic rights.
Spending that is kept in perpetuity for the public benefit. In Islamic civilisation, educational and medical institutions were founded on waqf.
Both words share a root meaning 'to increase'. Allah destroys usury, which seems to grow, and makes charity grow.
The natural disposition Allah created. The ustaz says most of us live against the fitrah in order to meet the needs of industry.
A river in Paradise granted to the Prophet ﷺ, also meaning 'abundance': his name and followers are always many.
The ability to convey broad meaning in brief words, one of the Prophet's ﷺ distinctions.
Harsh and rough. The trait of the angels of Hell in At-Tahrim 66:6, because their duty is to carry out punishment without mercy.

dalil.context: The ustaz uses it to show the great effect of losing a figure who played every role.
dalil.translation: Anas ibn Malik RA said the darkest day in Madinah was the day the Prophet ﷺ died, when everyone was gloomy and weeping.

dalil.context: The ustaz says hadith scholars graded it weak but not fabricated, and it is in line with Al-Baqarah 261. Jihad here includes wealth, life, time and energy.
dalil.translation: On that journey the Prophet ﷺ was shown a people who sowed and immediately harvested, and their crop increased without decreasing. Jibril explained they were those who strive in the way of Allah, their reward multiplied 700 times.

dalil.context: The believers have succeeded. The ustaz links 'falah' to the word for farmer, because we sow and are patient and may not live to harvest. The surah and verse number are not mentioned. (reference identified; verse number not mentioned)
The parable of those who spend their wealth in Allah's way is like a grain that grows seven ears, each ear a hundred grains. The ustaz says Ibn Kathir and other exegetes take 700 as a minimum.
dalil.translation: Those who spend their wealth in God’s cause are like grains of corn that produce seven ears, each bearing a hundred grains. God gives multiple increase to whoever He wishes: He is limitless and all knowing.

dalil.context: Allah destroys usury and makes charity grow. The ustaz stresses that 'riba' and 'yurbi' come from the same root.
dalil.translation: God blights usury, but blesses charitable deeds with multiple increase: He does not love the ungrateful sinner.

dalil.context: The ustaz says the Quran describes those who do not think as like cattle, even more astray, and prayer helps us think. The verse number is not mentioned. (reference identified; verse number not mentioned)
dalil.translation: We have created many jinn and people who are destined for Hell, with hearts they do not use for comprehension, eyes they do not use for sight, ears they do not use for hearing. They are like cattle, no, even further astray: these are the ones who are entirely heedless.

dalil.context: The first revelation 'Iqra'. The ustaz says scholars interpret it as reading not only texts but society and nature. The verse number is not mentioned. (reference identified; verse number not mentioned)
dalil.translation: Read! In the name of your Lord who created:

dalil.context: The ustaz links it to why prayer must not be abandoned under any circumstance.
dalil.translation: Islam is like a tent and prayer is its pole. If the pole breaks, the tent will not stand.

dalil.context: The prohibition on approaching prayer while intoxicated in the early phase of the prohibition of alcohol, because prayer demands full attention. (reference identified; verse number not mentioned)
dalil.translation: You who believe, do not come anywhere near the prayer if you are intoxicated, not until you know what you are saying; nor if you are in a state of major ritual impurity- though you may pass through the mosque- not until you have bathed; if you are ill, on a journey, have relieved yourselves, or had intercourse, and cannot find any water, then find some clean sand and wipe your faces and hands with it. God is always ready to pardon and forgive.

dalil.context: Mentioned as information; scholars differ on the details.
dalil.translation: Among the rivers the Prophet ﷺ saw were two rivers of Paradise and two on earth, the Nile and the Euphrates. Some scholars say the other two are Salsabil and a river that flows into Al-Kawthar.

dalil.context: Another narration in Bukhari says he was raised to the heavens and then reached that river.
dalil.translation: While walking in Paradise, the Prophet ﷺ came upon a river whose banks had domes of hollow pearl. He asked Jibril and was told, 'This is Al-Kawthar, which your Lord has granted you', and its soil smelled of musk.

dalil.context: Surah Al-Kawthar, revealed when the Prophet ﷺ was grieving the death of his son. Scholars link it to the river Al-Kawthar he saw. (reference identified; verse number not mentioned)
dalil.translation: We have truly given abundance to you [Prophet]––

dalil.context: It is the one who hates you who is cut off. The ustaz stresses that the Prophet's ﷺ name is always mentioned in the adhan, classes, remembrance and blessings. (reference identified; verse number not mentioned)
dalil.translation: it is the one who hates you who has been cut off.

dalil.context: The ustaz says in another narration the Prophet ﷺ saw colours he did not recognise.
dalil.translation: Its leaves were like elephant ears and its fruit like great jars. When it was covered by what Allah commanded, it changed so that no creature could describe its beauty.

dalil.context: The ustaz calls it a holistic picture of Paradise. The descriptions in the Quran, like fruit and rivers, are only what we can imagine.
dalil.translation: I have prepared for My righteous servants what no eye has seen, no ear has heard, and no human heart has conceived.

dalil.context: A part of the sirah narration told by the ustaz.
dalil.translation: No angel met me except laughing and glad, until I met an angel who did not smile.

dalil.context: The ustaz says this narration is in Ibn Ishaq's sirah and graded weak (not fabricated), but is supported by the Quranic verse (66:6) about the stern angels of Hell.
dalil.translation: Jibril explained the angel was Malik, keeper of Hell. If he had ever laughed at anyone, he would have laughed at the Prophet ﷺ, but he never smiles.

dalil.context: Protect yourselves and your families from the Fire, guarded by stern and harsh angels. The ustaz cites the Malay translation of Abdullah Basmeih (Pimpinan Ar-Rahman).
dalil.translation: Believers, guard yourselves and your families against a Fire fuelled by people and stones, over which stand angels, stern and strong; angels who never disobey God’s commands to them, but do as they are ordered:

dalil.context: Prayer prevents shameful and wrongful acts. The ustaz says the Quran itself states that prayer has a social impact. The surah and verse number are not mentioned. (reference identified; verse number not mentioned)
dalil.translation: [Prophet], recite what has been revealed to you of the Scripture; keep up the prayer: prayer restrains outrageous and unacceptable behaviour. Remembering God is greater: God knows everything you are doing.

sirah.summary: This episode continues the telling of what the Prophet ﷺ saw on the journey: the reward for those who spend, the river Al-Kawthar, Paradise and the keeper of Hell. The part on the zone Jibril cannot enter is deferred.

events.label: Reward
events.title: The Prophet ﷺ sees a people who harvest instantly
events.desc: Jibril explained they were those who strive in the way of Allah, their reward multiplied 700 times.

events.label: Paradise
events.title: The river Al-Kawthar with domes of pearl
events.desc: Its soil smelled of musk. The Prophet ﷺ asked and Jibril explained it was Allah's gift to him.

events.label: Mecca
events.title: Al-Kawthar revealed when the Prophet ﷺ grieved the loss of a son
events.desc: The Quraysh greeted him with the slogan 'Muhammad has been cut off', so Allah revealed that it was his enemy who would be cut off.

events.label: Sidrat al-Muntaha
events.title: The unrecognised colours of Paradise
events.desc: The Prophet ﷺ, the most eloquent (jawami' al-kalim), had no words to describe some of that beauty.

events.label: Lowest heaven
events.title: Welcomed gladly by every angel
events.desc: The Prophet ﷺ, the greatest guest, was welcomed with smiles and supplications.

events.label: Hell
events.title: Malik, keeper of Hell, does not smile
events.desc: A weak sirah narration but supported by a Quranic verse about the stern angels of Hell.
